catalog_quote: Vossen (1982, p. 193), in his phonological observations for Dongotono, Lokoya and Lopit together, states that there are four tones, consisting of High, Low, Mid, and High-Falling. ... the Mid tones observed by Vossen (1982) may be allotones of High or Low tones, given that the accompanying transcribed wordlist data (Vossen, 1982, pp. 126–149) suggests that they tend to occur in particular tonal contexts. [p. 69] For Dongotono, Lokoya and Lopit, Vossen (1982) records High, Low, Mid and High-Falling tones, as for Otuho. [p. 73, on Nilotic generally:] For the Southern and Eastern Nilotic languages, there is little mention of this possibility in later descriptive work, apart from some explicit statements that there is no contrastive stress, for example for Turkana (Heine, 1980, p. 44) and Otuho (Coates, 1985, p. 102).

new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is available. The only published phonological observation on Lokoya (Vossen 1982: 189-193, based on 1979 wordlist data from one speaker, reported here second-hand via Billington 2017 and Wikipedia) is that it is a tone language with four surface tones (H, L, M, HF) serving lexical and grammatical contrasts, with no contrastive vowel length; nothing is said about stress or accent.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Vossen (per Wikipedia's summary of pp. 189-193) warns the data are too limited for safe conclusions, and Billington suggests the Mid tone may be allotonic.
new_statements.domain_note: Second-hand tone inventory drawn from wordlist (citation-form) data covering Dongotono, Lokoya and Lopit together; not a stress statement and not specific to the word vs phrase domain.
new_statements.identity_note: Lokoya [lky, loko1254] = Westermann's 'Oxoriok' (Vossen 1982: 166 shows Westermann 1944: 19 places Oxoriok in the Lokoya villages Liria, Ilyangari, Langabu, Ngulere, although Tucker & Bryan 1956 used 'Koriok' for the 'Hill Lotuho' south of the Lotuko); the language has two sections, Lowoi and Loirya/Lerya (Driberg's 'Owe' and 'Lerya'). Muratori 1938 and its accent section describe Lotuxo = Otuho (otuh1238), not Lokoya; Billington 2017 and Moodie 2019 describe Lopit (lopi1242) and only report Vossen's Lokoya remarks second-hand.

tone_statements.quote: The following is a general description of the three languages in this study based on my fieldwork and on the work of Muratori (1938) and Westerman (1944). Lokoya, Lopit and Otuho have a nine-vowel system and display the Advanced Togue Root (ATR) feature, and a process of vowel harmony based on this feature. There are tones (at least High and Low), used for both lexical and grammatical distinctions. [...] The languages have a marked nominative case system with nominative and absolutive case. The nominative case is differentiated from the absolutive by a change in the tonal pattern across the noun. The case system is similar in Otuho and Lokoya.

sources.note: Its 'Accento' section (par. 49, 'In Lotuxo ci sono anche sillabe accentate, e sebbene l'accento non vi abbia quell'importanza che ha in altre lingue..') concerns Lotuxo = Otuho (otuh1238), not Lokoya. Lokoya appears only in ethnographic notes (Lowoi vs Telegu sections), a sub-dialect classification (Lokoya-Lano), a few comparative words (e.g. 'davanti: Lokoya fo xitemi') and a short Lokoya fable text (pp. 471-473); nothing on Lokoya stress or tone.

sources.note: First-hand but summary statement covering Lokoya, Lopit and Otuho together: 'There are tones (at least High and Low), used for both lexical and grammatical distinctions'; nominative case is distinguished from absolutive 'by a change in the tonal pattern across the noun', with the case system 'similar in Otuho and Lokoya' (p. 427). Examples are in broad phonetic transcription with tone marks; citation forms are given without tones because 'the tones in any particular utterance depend on a number of factors such as case, aspect, number' (p. 428). No tone inventory beyond 'at least High and Low'…
